cards.launderette: Launderette took over a 1950s laundromat on Holly Street in 2015 and has been a Michelin Guide listing and a neighborhood room ever since, with a new head chef in the kitchen since December. Order the plancha burger and the wood-grilled octopus, then finish with the birthday cake ice cream sandwich that Eater counts among Austin’s most iconic dishes. The neon sign out front does a lot of the work.
cards.hestia: Kevin Fink cooks over live fire at Hestia, and the room held a Michelin star in both 2024 and 2025. The scallops come off the hearth and the sourdough arrives with beef-fat butter, because everything here passes through the flame first. If the weekend included a personal best, this is the room where you tell the story.
cards.uchiko: Uchiko is Tyson Cole’s flagship sibling and the hardest table of the six, so book weeks out. Ham and eggs — crispy pork belly under a soft yolk — and the jasmine cream brûlée have been settling Austin arguments for fifteen years. Reserve it the same day you reserve the weekend tee times.
cards.sammies: Sammie’s Italian is the McGuire Moorman group’s red-sauce room, which means veal parm, martinis and a valet stand out front. The dining room runs to midnight on weekends. It is the right answer when the second eighteen finished at seven and the evening still needs to feel like an occasion.
cards.este: Este comes from the Suerte team and cooks coastal Mexican seafood — aguachiles, wood-fired whole fish — out of the prettiest blue building on the east side. The reservation is the hard part. The hour on the patio once you have it is the easiest thing about the whole weekend.
cards.clarks: Clark’s is a tiny preppy-nautical room on West 6th that has been the city’s default celebration spot since 2012. Order oysters, a lobster roll and something cold and French by the glass. The room is small enough that the reservation is the hard part, though the bar seats reward walk-in optimism.
cards.josephine: Josephine House sits in a blue cottage in Clarksville with a gravel garden patio, next door to its sister restaurant Jeffrey’s. This is the golden-hour option, so go before sunset and take a table outside. The steak frites and the string lights will do the apologizing for a five-hour absence.
cards.oddduck: Odd Duck is Bryce Gilmore’s farm-to-table original and a Michelin Bib Gourmand, and it started life as a trailer before it turned into an institution. The small plates are the best ordering in town. The move is to hand the menu back and ask the kitchen to feed you.
cards.justines: Justine’s runs out of a 1937 bungalow in candlelight, seats late and pours later. Steak frites, escargot and a bottle of red arrive with no rush attached to any of it. When the second round ran long and every other kitchen in town is closing, Justine’s is the insurance policy.
cards.canje: Canje is Tavel Bristol-Joseph’s modern Caribbean room, where pepper fish and West Indian curry come out of the kitchen and the rum drinks come off the bar. It is loud, warm and fully alive. Food & Wine ranked it No. 3 on the 2026 Global Tastemakers list.
cards.tfb: A fire took the 1981 institution down in January 2022, and Texas French Bread reopened on Rio Grande this spring, four and a half years later. Dinner service runs Tuesday through Saturday, farm-to-table, with lamb meatballs and trout with braised cabbage on the menu. Bring someone who understands why that matters.
cards.birdies: Birdie’s is a counter-service wine bar whose name settles where you go after a round with birdies in it. Food & Wine named it Restaurant of the Year in 2023, and both halves of the couple who run it hold Beard nominations. Seasonal pastas and an olive-oil soft-serve sundae draw a line that forms before the doors open.
cards.loro: Loro is Aaron Franklin and Tyson Cole’s Asian smokehouse, which means smoked brisket with chili gastrique, oak-grilled ribs and frozen drinks under a big shaded patio. Nobody takes a reservation and nobody minds sandals. It works when date night has to start twenty minutes after the last putt.
cards.nixta: Edgar Rico runs an heirloom-masa taqueria with a James Beard Best Emerging Chef award and a TIME100 nod behind it, and the cooking carries both: duck carnitas tacos, a beet “tartare” tostada. Nixta is casual in its price and its dress code and nowhere else.
cards.matts: Matt’s El Rancho has been serving Tex-Mex since 1952, and it is the answer for the partner who wants a Bob Armstrong queso and a frozen margarita rather than a tasting menu and a recap of your back nine. The place closes on Tuesdays and there will be a wait, and the wait is part of the arrangement.

kickers.1: The full-apology tier runs from a Michelin star to the hardest sushi table in town, by way of red-sauce glamour and the converted laundromat that started the idea. Book these when you book the tee times, not after.
kickers.2: These rooms are special without the ceremony: garden patios, candlelit brasseries, a Caribbean room on a global best-of list and the best comeback story in Austin dining. Most of them can absorb a same-day plan.
kickers.3: The second eighteen takes something out of you, and these four ask for nothing back: walk-in wine bars, smoked brisket with a patio, Beard-winning tacos and fifty-year-old queso. One of them is named Birdie’s.
